title: The Portion of Labor
description: Published in 1901 and Freeman's most ambitious novel: a New England shoe-manufacturing town, a strike and a young woman's choice.
plot_or_argument: Ellen Brewster, a factory girl of talent, is loved by the mill owner's son and by a young socialist; when the strike comes she must choose between her class and her love, and the novel ends with her refusing the rich marriage and committing herself to the work of the town.
historical_context: 1901: the New England shoe industry, the labor wars of the 1890s, the socialist movement of the new century, and the American debate on the 'woman question'.
literary_significance: The Portion of Labor is Freeman's most ambitious book and one of the first American novels to treat the factory girl as a serious subject: its analysis of class and its refusal of the conventional marriage ending made it a landmark of American industrial fiction and a bridge between the regional story and the American social novel.

title: Violets and Other Tales
description: Published in 1895 and the first book by an African-American woman from the deep South: stories, sketches and poems of Creole New Orleans.
plot_or_argument: The volume mixes short stories of New Orleans life with lyrics on love, death and the poet's vocation, and closes with an essay on the position of women, presenting a Creole world in which race, class and desire are entangled.
historical_context: 1895: the Creole society of New Orleans, the emergence of the black woman writer, and the literary culture of the black press of the 1890s.
literary_significance: Violets and Other Tales is the first book by an African-American woman of the deep South and a founding text of African-American women's literature: its portraits of Creole life and its lyrics on love and ambition made Dunbar-Nelson one of the most important black writers of the 1890s.

title: The Goodness of St Rocque and Other Stories
description: Published in 1899 and the first collection of short stories by an African-American woman: Creole New Orleans, the colour line and the lives of women.
plot_or_argument: The stories present the mixed-race society of New Orleans — the quadroon ball, the young woman who passes for white, the nun who protects a girl, the old woman who keeps a shrine — in narratives that turn on the gradations of colour and class within black and Creole society.
historical_context: 1895-99: the racial hierarchy of New Orleans, the tests of the colour line, and the black literary market of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Goodness of St Rocque is the first book of short stories by an African-American woman and the finest literary treatment of the Creole colour hierarchy: its analysis of intraracial colour prejudice made it a unique text in the period, and it is a founding document of African-American women's fiction.

title: Mine Eyes Have Seen
description: Published in 1918 and the only play by Dunbar-Nelson: a black soldier's family waits for news on the eve of his departure for France.
plot_or_argument: A black American family debates whether the son should go to fight in the First World War; the mother remembers slavery, the father argues for the country that has denied them citizenship, and the son leaves for France with the hope that his service will earn the rights the family has never had.
historical_context: 1918: the First World War, the Great Migration, the hopes of black soldiers in 1917-18, and the American debate on 'making the world safe for democracy'.
literary_significance: Mine Eyes Have Seen is one of the earliest published plays by an African-American woman and the central black American dramatic text of the First World War: its argument about citizenship, service and the colour line made it a landmark of African-American drama.

title: Mrs Spring Fragrance and Other Writings
description: Published in 1912 and the first book of fiction about Chinese America: stories of San Francisco's Chinatown and the Chinese-American household.
plot_or_argument: The stories follow Mrs Spring Fragrance and her husband in their San Francisco flat, the Chinese merchant and his Americanised son, the white woman who marries a Chinese man, and the children of the Chinatown schools, presenting the immigrant world from the inside and the misunderstandings of the white world from outside.
historical_context: 1890-1912: the Chinese Exclusion Act, the San Francisco Chinatown, the anti-Chinese agitation of the 1890s, and the American debate on immigration and race.
literary_significance: Mrs Spring Fragrance is the founding text of Asian-American literature: it was the first book of fiction in English to present Chinese immigrants as human beings rather than as the 'yellow peril' of the newspapers, and its mixed-race perspective made it a unique document in the American literature of immigration.

title: 'Leaves from the Mental Portfolio of an Eurasian'
description: Published in 1909 and the founding Asian-American autobiography: a Eurasian writer's account of her divided inheritance and her decision to speak for the Chinese.
plot_or_argument: Eaton recounts her English childhood, her Chinese mother, the prejudice she met in Montreal and San Francisco, her work as a journalist, and the moment when she chose to identify herself publicly as Chinese rather than pass as white, in order to write on behalf of the immigrant community.
historical_context: 1909: the Chinese Exclusion Act, the assimilation debate of the 1900s, and the American magazine market for immigrant autobiography.
literary_significance: 'Leaves from the Mental Portfolio of an Eurasian' is the first Asian-American autobiography and a central document of American multiracial identity: its account of the choice to claim a stigmatised ancestry made it a founding text of Asian-American literature and of the American literature of passing.

title: Yekl: A Tale of the New York Ghetto
description: Published in 1896 and the first English fiction of the Jewish immigrant: a Russian Jew's Americanisation and the wife he has left behind.
plot_or_argument: Yekl, a young Russian Jew, has become 'Jake' in the New York ghetto, with American clothes, American manners and an American girl; when his wife Gitl arrives from Russia with their son, he is ashamed of her old-world appearance, and the novella ends with the divorce that leaves Gitl alone in the new world.
historical_context: 1896: the mass immigration of Russian Jews, the Lower East Side ghetto, the sweatshop, and the American debate on assimilation.
literary_significance: Yekl is the first English fiction of the Jewish immigrant and the founding text of the Jewish-American novel: its portrait of the immigrant who is ashamed of his own wife, and its recording of the mixed English of the ghetto, made it the model for the American immigrant novel, and Howells praised it as the finest American story of the year.

title: The Rise of David Levinsky
description: Published in 1917 and the greatest American immigrant novel: a Russian yeshiva student becomes a millionaire in the garment trade and finds that success is emptiness.
plot_or_argument: David Levinsky arrives in New York in 1882 penniless, works in a sweatshop, studies at night, and rises through the cloak-and-suit trade to become a millionaire manufacturer; at the height of his success he looks back on the faith, the mother and the love he has lost, and finds that he would give it all to be a poor yeshiva student again.
principal_characters: David Levinsky; Dora; Matilda; Gitelson; Mrs Levinsky; Shiphrah; Meyer Nudelman
historical_context: 1882-1917: the Russian pogroms, the Jewish immigration, the garment industry of New York, and the American ideology of the self-made man.
literary_significance: The Rise of David Levinsky is the greatest American immigrant novel and one of the central American novels of success: its analysis of the cost of Americanisation, its portrait of the garment trade and its plain, unhurried prose made it the model for the American ethnic novel, and it is the finest fictional record of Jewish immigrant life in America.

title: The Imported Bridegroom and Other Stories
description: Published in 1898 and the best of Cahan's stories: the immigrant generation and its children in the New York ghetto.
plot_or_argument: The title story follows Flora, an Americanised Jewish girl whose father imports a bridegroom from Russia, a young Talmudist who is then seduced by the philosophy of Spencer; the other stories present the sweatshop, the synagogue, the boarding house and the socialist meeting of the Lower East Side.
historical_context: 1897-98: the Lower East Side, the socialist and Zionist movements of the immigrant community, and the American magazine market for the short story.
literary_significance: The Imported Bridegroom is the finest American story collection of Jewish immigrant life before the twentieth century: its title story is a small masterpiece of generational conflict, and the book established the short story as the natural form of the American immigrant experience.

title: Sister Carrie
description: Published in 1900 and the founding American naturalist novel of the city: a country girl's rise in Chicago and New York through the men who desire her.
plot_or_argument: Carrie Meeber comes from a Wisconsin village to Chicago, works in a shoe factory, is taken up by the salesman Drouet and then by the saloon manager Hurstwood; Hurstwood steals money and flees with her to New York, where he declines into poverty and suicide while Carrie becomes a successful actress.
principal_characters: Carrie Meeber; Charles Drouet; George Hurstwood; Julia Hurstwood; Minnie Hanson; Robert Ames; Lola Osborne
historical_context: 1900: the Chicago of the 1890s, the department store and the new consumption, the Broadway theatre, and the American debate on the 'woman adrift'.
literary_significance: Sister Carrie is the founding American naturalist novel and the first great American novel of the city: its refusal to punish Carrie, its sympathy for Hurstwood and its cold analysis of desire made it a scandal in 1900 and the model for the twentieth-century American novel.

title: Jennie Gerhardt
description: Published in 1911 and Dreiser's most sympathetic novel: a poor German girl's life of sacrifice for her family and the men who love her.
plot_or_argument: Jennie Gerhardt, the daughter of a poor Ohio family, is seduced by the senator Brander and then becomes the mistress of Lester Kane, a rich manufacturer; she gives up Kane when his family and his ambitions demand it, raises her daughter, and ends the novel in quiet poverty, having been generous to everyone who used her.
principal_characters: Jennie Gerhardt; Lester Kane; William Gerhardt; Senator Brander; Robert Kane; Letty Pace; Vesta
historical_context: 1911: the German immigrant poor of the Midwest, the class system of the 1880s-1900s, the double standard, and the American debate on the 'fallen woman'.
literary_significance: Jennie Gerhardt is the most humane American naturalist novel and the finest American portrait of a woman's lifelong self-sacrifice: its refusal to condemn Jennie made it a landmark of American fiction, and it is the book in which Dreiser's sympathy and his determinism are most completely reconciled.

title: The Financier
description: Published in 1912 and the first American novel of the financier: the rise and fall of a Philadelphia street-railway magnate.
plot_or_argument: Frank Cowperwood, a young Philadelphia broker, makes a fortune in street railways and city finance, is caught in the panic of 1871 and convicted of embezzlement, serves thirteen months in prison and emerges with his ambition intact, while his wife and his mistress wait for him outside.
principal_characters: Frank Cowperwood; Lillian Cowperwood; Aileen Butler; Edward Butler; Peter Laughlin; Stener; Harper Steger
historical_context: 1912: the Philadelphia of the 1860s-70s, the panic of 1871 and the great Chicago fire, the corruption of city politics, and the American cult of the 'captain of industry'.
literary_significance: The Financier is the first great American novel of finance and the founding text of the American business novel: its portrait of Cowperwood, based on the street-railway magnate Charles Yerkes, made the amoral financier a central American literary figure, and it is the essential American fiction of the Gilded Age economy.

title: An American Tragedy
description: Published in 1925 and the greatest American naturalist novel: a young man murders the factory girl he has made pregnant in order to marry a rich woman.
plot_or_argument: Clyde Griffiths, the son of street preachers, goes to work in his uncle's collar factory, seduces the factory girl Roberta Alden, and falls in love with the rich Sondra Finchley; he takes Roberta to a lake in the Adirondacks intending to murder her, and though his nerve fails, she drowns, and he is tried, condemned and executed.
principal_characters: Clyde Griffiths; Roberta Alden; Sondra Finchley; Hortense Briggs; Samuel Griffiths; Asa Griffiths; Belknap; Jephson
historical_context: 1925: the American small town and the factory city of the 1920s, the class barriers of American life, the Chester Gillette-Grace Brown murder case of 1906, and the American debate on capital punishment.
literary_significance: An American Tragedy is the masterpiece of American naturalism and one of the central American novels of the century: its patient, documentary accumulation and its refusal of moral judgement made it the fullest expression of Dreiser's determinism, and it is the great American novel of class and desire.

title: Democracy: An American Novel
description: Published anonymously in 1880 and the sharpest American political novel of the Gilded Age: a clever widow's education in the corruption of Washington.
plot_or_argument: Madeleine Lee, a rich and intelligent young widow from New York, comes to Washington to understand power; she is courted by the honest Senator Ratcliffe, the cynical Mr French and the young John Carrington, and discovers that the man who can govern is also the man who has taken a bribe, and leaves the city in disillusion.
principal_characters: Madeleine Lee; Senator Silas P. Ratcliffe; John Carrington; Mr French; Lord Skye; Mrs Lee; Sybil Ross
historical_context: 1880: the Washington of the Grant era, the Credit Mobilier and the Tweed scandals, the spoils system, and the American debate on the fitness of democracy.
literary_significance: Democracy is the finest American political novel of the nineteenth century: its portrait of Washington and its analysis of the relation between power and corruption made it a sensation when it appeared anonymously, and it remains the essential American novel of the capital.

title: The Education of Henry Adams
description: Printed privately in 1907 and published in 1918: the greatest American autobiography, and the central American meditation on the modern world.
plot_or_argument: Adams tells his own life in the third person as the education of a man who was never educated: Harvard, the London legation during the Civil War, Washington, the writing of history, the failure of his marriage, and the discovery — in front of the dynamo at the Paris Exposition of 1900 — that the modern world has replaced the unity of the Virgin with the force of the machine.
historical_context: 1838-1905: the American political dynasty of the Adamses, the Civil War, the Gilded Age, the Darwinian revolution, and the technology of the dynamo and the radio.
literary_significance: The Education of Henry Adams is the greatest American autobiography and one of the central texts of modern American thought: its theory of the dynamo and the Virgin, its third-person narrative and its account of the failure of education have made it the essential American meditation on modernity, and it won the Pulitzer Prize in 1919.

title: Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres
description: Privately printed in 1904 and published in 1913: Adams's study of the medieval imagination, the companion to The Education.
plot_or_argument: Adams reads the architecture, the glass, the sculpture and the poetry of twelfth- and thirteenth-century France — Mont-Saint-Michel, Chartres, the Song of Roland, the troubadours, the cult of the Virgin — as the expression of a unity of feeling and belief that the modern world has lost.
historical_context: 1900-04: the medieval revival of the 1890s, the Catholic aesthetics of the period, and the American study of the Middle Ages after Ruskin.
literary_significance: Mont-Saint-Michel and Chartres is one of the great American works of cultural criticism and the essential companion to The Education of Henry Adams: its reading of the medieval world as a unity of faith and art made it a founding text of American medieval studies and the source of Adams's central metaphor of the Virgin and the dynamo.

title: History of the United States during the Administrations of Jefferson and Madison
description: Published in nine volumes from 1889 to 1891 and the greatest American historical work of the century: the United States from 1800 to 1817.
plot_or_argument: Adams narrates the Jefferson and Madison administrations from the election of 1800 to the end of the war of 1812: the Louisiana Purchase, the embargo, the rise of the war party, the burning of Washington and the peace of Ghent, with the growth of American nationality as the underlying theme.
historical_context: 1800-17 and 1889: the early republic, the Napoleonic wars, the War of 1812, and the late nineteenth-century American debate on national character.
literary_significance: The History is the greatest American historical narrative of the nineteenth century: its research, its irony and its analysis of the growth of American nationality made it the model of American historical writing, and it remains the standard account of the Jefferson and Madison administrations.

title: American Indian Stories
description: Published in 1921 and the founding text of modern Native American literature: the autobiographical stories and political essays of a Yankton Dakota woman.
plot_or_argument: The book opens with 'Impressions of an Indian Childhood', in which a girl is raised in the Dakota way, then 'The School Days of an Indian Girl', in which she is taken to a white boarding school where her hair is cut and her language forbidden, and ends with the political essays on the land and the Bureau of Indian Affairs.
historical_context: 1900-21: the Indian boarding schools, the allotment policy and the Dawes Act, the Society of American Indians, and the campaign for Native citizenship.
literary_significance: American Indian Stories is the first Native American woman's autobiography and the founding text of modern Native American literature: its account of the boarding-school trauma and its political essays made it a central document of American Indian history, and it is the book from which modern Native American writing begins.

title: Old Indian Legends
description: Published in 1901 and the first collection of Native American legends by a Native American author: fourteen Dakota stories of the trickster Iktomi and the great deeds of the old world.
plot_or_argument: The collection retells the Dakota stories of Iktomi the spider-trickster and his schemes, of the buffalo and the prairie, of the great hunter and the sky, in versions taken from the oral tradition and retold for an English-reading audience while keeping the cadence of the original.
historical_context: 1901: the American vogue for the Indian legend after Longfellow and Schoolcraft, the boarding-school experience, and the ethnographic collection of Native oral literature.
literary_significance: Old Indian Legends is the first collection of Native American legends by a Native American author and the founding text of Native American literary translation: its versions of the Iktomi stories preserved the oral tradition at the moment of its destruction, and it established the model for all later Native American retellings.

title: 'Why I Am a Pagan'
description: Published in 1902 and the most important Native American essay of the period: a defence of Dakota religion against Christian conversion.
plot_or_argument: Zitkala-Sa describes sitting in church while a missionary preaches, remembering her mother's prayer to the Great Spirit in the open air, and explains why she cannot accept a faith that has been forced on her people and that treats the Dakota religion as heathen superstition.
historical_context: 1902: the Christian missionary campaign among Native Americans, the Atlantic Monthly and the reform press, and the Native American response to assimilation.
literary_significance: 'Why I Am a Pagan' is the central Native American essay of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries: its defence of Dakota religion and its critique of missionary Christianity made it a founding text of Native American intellectual resistance, and it is one of the earliest direct statements of Native American religious freedom.

title: The Woman Who Did
description: Published in 1895 and the most scandalous New Woman novel of the decade: a woman who refuses marriage and lives openly with the man she loves.
plot_or_argument: Herminia Barton, a Cambridge-educated woman of principle, agrees to live with Alan Merrick without marriage because she believes the marriage law degrades women; after his death she raises their daughter alone, is ostracised by respectable society, and finally takes her own life so that her daughter may marry respectably.
principal_characters: Herminia Barton; Alan Merrick; Dolores Barton; Dr Merrick; Miss Barton; the vicar
historical_context: 1895: the campaign for the reform of marriage law, the feminist circles of the 1890s, the Wilde trials and the moral panic of 1895, and the debate on the 'free union'.
literary_significance: The Woman Who Did was the most radical New Woman novel of the century and the most discussed book of 1895: its heroine's refusal of marriage, its frank treatment of unmarried motherhood and its tragic ending made it a national scandal, and it remains the central text of the argument over free union in the 1890s.

title: The British Barbarians
description: Published in 1895 and Allen's satirical anthropology of English life: a visitor from the twenty-fifth century observes the barbarism of the Victorian suburb.
plot_or_argument: Bertram Ingledew, a traveller from a future civilisation, arrives in a Surrey suburb and studies its inhabitants as an anthropologist; he records their taboos — the worship of respectability, the ritual of the Sunday, the sacrifice of women to the marriage law, the fetish of property — and finally leaves them to their barbarism.
historical_context: 1895: the vogue of the scientific utopia after Bellamy and Morris, the anthropology of the 1890s, and the New Woman debate on marriage and the family.
literary_significance: The British Barbarians is the most effective English satirical utopia of the 1890s and the model for the modern anthropological satire of one's own society: its device of the future observer among the suburban Victorians made it a landmark of English social criticism, and it is one of the funniest and most radical books of its decade.

title: The Evolution of the Idea of God
description: Published in 1897 and Allen's major work of evolutionary anthropology: an inquiry into the origin and development of the idea of God.
plot_or_argument: Allen traces the idea of a deity from the ghost-fear and ancestor-worship of early humanity through the fetish, the nature-god and the tribal deity to the monotheism of the civilised world, arguing that religion is a natural evolutionary product and that its history can be studied like any other human institution.
historical_context: 1897: the evolutionary anthropology of Tylor and Spencer, the Victorian debate on the origin of religion, and the freethought movement of the 1890s.
literary_significance: The Evolution of the Idea of God is the most complete English statement of the evolutionary theory of religion: it brought the methods of anthropology to the central question of Victorian belief, it provoked a storm of controversy, and it is a key document of the Victorian secularisation of thought.

title: Physiological Aesthetics
description: Published in 1877 and Allen's first book and the founding English work of scientific aesthetics: an attempt to explain the experience of beauty in physiological terms.
plot_or_argument: Allen argues that the pleasure of beauty is the pleasure of an easy and healthy exercise of the nervous system: that the beautiful is what the eye and the brain can take in without strain, and that the arts must therefore be understood as the deliberate production of that physiological state.
historical_context: 1877: the new physiology of Helmholtz and Grant Allen's own science teaching, the aesthetics of Ruskin and Pater, and the Victorian attempt to found a science of the mind.
literary_significance: Physiological Aesthetics is the founding work of evolutionary aesthetics in English and one of the first scientific accounts of aesthetic experience: it anticipated the modern psychology of art by a century, it influenced Vernon Lee and the whole tradition of physiological criticism, and it is a landmark of Victorian scientific thought.

title: Miss Cayley's Adventures
description: Published in 1899 and the most entertaining of Allen's New Woman books: a penniless, clever woman makes her way round the world and solves a mystery on the way.
plot_or_argument: Lois Cayley, left without money, sets out to earn her living: she becomes a lady's companion in Florence, a typist in London, a nurse and a traveller, outwits a series of swindlers, and finally solves the mystery of a missing Rajah's treasure and marries the man who has followed her.
historical_context: 1898-99: the new employment of women, the tourist route to Italy and India, the imperial world of the 1890s, and the demand for the female detective story after Sherlock Holmes.
literary_significance: Miss Cayley's Adventures is one of the most enjoyable New Woman novels of the decade and an early female detective narrative: its heroine's professional adventures made it a model for the twentieth-century woman's travel novel, and it shows Allen's feminism in its most attractive form.
